stem: The oxidation number of chromium in potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇, is
explanation: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 gives 2x = 12, so x = +6. +12 is the total for both chromium atoms, and +3 is chromium's oxidation number after dichromate has been reduced.

stem: 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 250 cm³. Its molarity is (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
explanation: Moles of NaOH = 4.0/40 = 0.1 mol, and volume = 0.250 dm³, so M = 0.1/0.250 = 0.4 M. 0.1 M forgets that the volume is only a quarter of a litre, and 0.016 M divides grams by cm³.

stem: 9.0 g of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆, molar mass 180 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in 250 g of water. The molality of the solution is
explanation: Moles of glucose = 9.0/180 = 0.05 mol, and mass of solvent = 0.250 kg, so molality = 0.05/0.250 = 0.2 mol kg⁻¹. 0.05 m is just the number of moles, which ignores the mass of water.

stem: The vapour pressure of a pure solvent is 30 torr. A non-volatile solute is dissolved so that the mole fraction of the solvent is 0.9. By Raoult's law, the vapour pressure of the solution is
explanation: Raoult's law: p = x(solvent) × p° = 0.9 × 30 = 27 torr. 3 torr is the lowering of vapour pressure, not the vapour pressure itself, and a non-volatile solute can never raise it to 33 torr.

stem: Colligative properties of a dilute solution depend mainly on
options: the chemical nature of the solute
the molar mass of the solvent alone
explanation: Colligative properties (vapour-pressure lowering, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression, osmotic pressure) depend on how many solute particles are present, not on what they are. That is why 0.1 m NaCl has about twice the effect of 0.1 m glucose.

stem: 0.5 mol of sodium chloride is dissolved in 1 kg of water. Assuming complete dissociation and Kb (water) = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹, the boiling point of the solution is
explanation: NaCl gives two ions, so the particle molality is 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 m and ΔTb = 0.52 × 1.0 = 0.52 K, giving 100.52 °C. 100.26 °C ignores dissociation, and 99.48 °C wrongly lowers the boiling point.

stem: Which aqueous solution has the lowest freezing point?
explanation: Freezing-point depression is proportional to the molality of particles: CaCl₂ gives 3 ions (0.3 m), NaCl gives 2 (0.2 m), while glucose and urea do not ionise (0.1 m). The largest depression means the lowest freezing point, so CaCl₂.

stem: During the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride, the product formed at the cathode is
explanation: The cathode is where reduction happens: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na. Chlorine forms at the anode by oxidation of Cl⁻. Hydrogen appears only when water is present, as in the electrolysis of brine.

stem: A charge of 0.2 faraday is passed through copper(II) sulphate solution. The mass of copper deposited at the cathode is (Cu = 63.5)
explanation: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so 2 F deposit 1 mol of Cu; 0.2 F deposit 0.1 mol = 6.35 g. 12.7 g assumes one faraday per mole of copper, ignoring the 2+ charge.

stem: Standard electrode potentials: Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V and Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V. The standard emf of the Daniell cell, Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu, is
explanation: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V, with copper as the cathode. 0.42 V comes from ignoring the negative sign of the zinc potential, and a working galvanic cell has a positive emf.

stem: In a galvanic (voltaic) cell, oxidation takes place at the
explanation: Oxidation always occurs at the anode; in a galvanic cell the anode releases electrons into the external circuit, so it is the negative electrode. In electrolysis the anode is positive, which is why the third option is a common confusion.

stem: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻ oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ and is itself reduced to Mn²⁺. The number of moles of Fe²⁺ oxidised by one mole of MnO₄⁻ is
explanation: Manganese goes from +7 to +2, gaining 5 electrons, while each Fe²⁺ loses only 1 electron, so one MnO₄⁻ oxidises 5 Fe²⁺: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O. Choosing 1 ignores electron balance.

stem: Standard reduction potentials: Li⁺/Li = −3.04 V, Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V, Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V, Ag⁺/Ag = +0.80 V. The strongest reducing agent among these metals is
explanation: The most negative reduction potential means the metal gives up electrons most readily, so lithium is the strongest reducing agent. Silver has the most positive potential, so Ag⁺ is the strongest oxidising agent, and Ag is the weakest reducing agent.

stem: Galvanised iron (iron coated with zinc) does not rust even when the coating is scratched, because
options: zinc is less reactive than iron and never corrodes
zinc is oxidised in preference to iron
zinc reduces the rust back to iron metal
zinc stops oxygen from dissolving in water
explanation: Zinc has a more negative electrode potential than iron, so it acts as the anode and is oxidised instead of iron (sacrificial protection). Zinc is more reactive than iron, not less; tin plating, by contrast, protects only while unbroken.

stem: During the discharge of a lead–acid accumulator,
options: the sulphuric acid becomes more concentrated and denser
lead dioxide is formed on both of the electrodes
lead at the negative plate is reduced to lead sulphate
lead sulphate forms on both plates and the acid gets diluted
explanation: On discharge, Pb is oxidised to PbSO₄ at the negative plate and PbO₂ is reduced to PbSO₄ at the positive plate; both reactions use up H₂SO₄ and produce water, so the acid's density falls. Lead going to Pb²⁺ is oxidation, not reduction.

stem: The oxidation number of sulphur in the thiosulphate ion, S₂O₃²⁻, is
explanation: 2x + 3(−2) = −2 gives 2x = +4, so the average oxidation number is +2. +2.5 is the value in the tetrathionate ion S₄O₆²⁻, and +6 is the value in sulphate.

stem: A current of 5.0 A is passed through silver nitrate solution. The time needed to deposit 1.08 g of silver is (Ag = 108; F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
explanation: 1.08 g = 0.01 mol Ag, and Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag needs 0.01 F = 965 C. Time = Q/I = 965/5.0 = 193 s. 965 s is the charge in coulombs mistaken for time.

stem: A solution is made by mixing 36 g of water with 46 g of ethanol, C₂H₅OH. The mole fraction of water in the solution is (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
explanation: Water = 36/18 = 2 mol and ethanol = 46/46 = 1 mol, so x(water) = 2/(2 + 1) = 0.67. 0.44 is the mass fraction 36/82, and 0.33 is the mole fraction of ethanol.
